title: Sore Eye - Telephone Triage of Orbital Cellulitis
patient_instructions: You are Jane, a 34-year-old woman phoning your GP because you are frightened about your eye. This is a telephone consultation - you cannot be seen, only heard. Speak first: 'Doctor, it's been two days, I've got really bad pain in my eye and now it's all swollen shut, I'm scared.' Story if asked: two days ago while gardening a tree branch fell and scratched your face just above the eyebrow. Since then the eye has been red and increasingly painful, and now the eyelid is so swollen it has closed the eye completely. You feel hot and cold (possibly feverish) and have a headache. If asked whether it hurts to move the eye - say yes, it is painful. Because the eye is shut you cannot comment on your vision or whether the eye looks pushed forward. You do NOT wear contact lenses. No burning, no discharge, no itch. Your idea: 'maybe I've just got an infection in my eyelid.' Your concern: you are scared and want to know if it is serious. Your expectation: advice on what to do. Affect: anxious, a little short of breath from worry. If the candidate tells you to go to the Emergency Department now, agree and ask how you should get there.
candidate_instructions: You are the GP. You open the consulting room door, the examiner performs an ID check and leaves, and you pick up a ringing telephone. On the line is Jane, a 34-year-old woman who is concerned about her eye. Over 8 minutes: take a focused telephone history (about 5 minutes), then explain to Jane your most likely diagnosis and differentials, and outline your immediate management and disposition. You have no physical examination available - this is a telephone triage station.
examiner_instructions: This is a telephone triage station where correct disposition scores the marks. The must-not-miss diagnosis is orbital (post-septal) cellulitis - a sight- and life-threatening emergency - given the traumatic entry point from tree/plant material, severe swelling shutting the eye, systemic upset and pain on eye movement. Reward candidates who actively screen (even by phone) for orbital red flags: painful AND restricted eye movements/ophthalmoplegia, proptosis, reduced or lost vision, diplopia, colour-vision loss (ask 'can you read text at all?', 'does the eye look pushed forward?'). The safety-critical management is: send to ED NOW via ambulance (000) if no driver - patient must not drive - for urgent ophthalmology AND ENT review, empirical IV antibiotics started immediately, with CT orbits/sinuses obtained urgently but NOT delaying antibiotics. Fail the safety domain if the candidate delays disposition for imaging or manages as a minor eyelid infection.

criteria: Telephone-appropriate opening: introduces self, confirms who is speaking, gains consent to ask questions
Characterises pain (SIQOORA) and specifically asks about pain on eye movement and pain on blinking
Screens eyelid, eye and systemic symptoms (swelling, discharge, vision, photophobia, fever, headache, sinus/flu symptoms)
Elicits risk factors: gardening/plant trauma, contact lenses, occupation, recent injury
Identifies orbital cellulitis as the leading must-not-miss diagnosis given trauma, swelling, systemic upset and painful eye movement
Actively screens for orbital red flags (ophthalmoplegia, proptosis, visual loss, RAPD, diplopia, chemosis, colour-vision loss) to separate orbital from preseptal
Offers a sensible differential: preseptal cellulitis, endophthalmitis, corneal ulcer, and broader red-eye causes
Immediate disposition to ED now; ambulance via 000 if no driver, patient not to drive herself
States urgent ophthalmology AND ENT referral with empirical IV antibiotics started immediately, NOT delayed for imaging
CT orbits/sinuses/brain and bloods (FBC, ESR, CRP) obtained urgently; considers tetanus given plant-material injury
Explains diagnosis and urgency clearly and calmly in plain language, acknowledging fear
Gives clear safety-netting and confirms the patient understands to attend ED immediately

red_flags: Pain on AND restriction of eye movement (ophthalmoplegia) - hallmark distinguishing orbital from preseptal cellulitis
Proptosis (eye pushed forward), reduced/lost visual acuity, relative afferent pupillary defect, diplopia, chemosis or colour-vision loss
Penetrating/plant-material facial or ocular injury as an infective entry point (tree branch while gardening)
Systemic upset (fever, headache) with eyelid swelling closing the eye - severe infection, risk of subperiosteal abscess, cavernous sinus thrombosis, intracranial spread
Any reduction in vision - 'always test and record vision' - escalates urgency
australian_guidelines: Therapeutic Guidelines (eTG) - orbital cellulitis requires urgent empirical IV antibiotics (e.g. flucloxacillin plus ceftriaxone, add metronidazole if sinus/abscess source); antibiotics must not be delayed for imaging
Therapeutic Guidelines (eTG) - preseptal cellulitis may be managed with oral antibiotics (e.g. amoxicillin-clavulanate) with close review, in contrast to orbital cellulitis
Emergency disposition - call 000 for ambulance transfer to ED; patient must not drive; urgent combined ophthalmology and ENT review
Murtagh red-eye golden rule - always test and record visual acuity in any painful/red eye; tetanus prophylaxis considered for penetrating plant-material wounds
learning_objectives: Conduct a structured telephone history for an acutely painful eye and reach a safe disposition decision
Differentiate orbital (post-septal) from preseptal cellulitis using red-flag symptoms
Recognise plant/tree trauma as a dangerous ocular infective entry point
Initiate emergency management: IV antibiotics started before/alongside urgent CT, combined ophthalmology and ENT referral
key_points: In suspected orbital cellulitis, start empirical IV antibiotics and refer urgently to ophthalmology AND ENT - do NOT delay treatment for the CT scan.
Painful and restricted eye movement is the pivotal feature that turns a swollen red eye into a sight-threatening emergency.
Orbital cellulitis is commoner in children, usually secondary to ethmoid sinusitis, and can progress to subperiosteal abscess and cavernous sinus thrombosis.
On the phone you cannot examine - so ask proxy questions for red flags: can she read text, does the eye look pushed forward, does moving the eye hurt.

citations.claim: A red, tender eye is a very common presentation; an accurate history plus examination usually allows diagnosis, with serious not-to-be-missed disorders forming part of the diagnostic strategy for the red and tender eye.
citations.source: John Murtagh General Practice, 8th Edition.pdf, p.1171

citations.claim: Painful-eye differentials include acute glaucoma and iritis/optic neuritis.
citations.source: John Murtagh General Practice, 8th Edition.pdf, p.1212

citations.claim: Peri-orbital oedema and regional (pre-auricular/head and neck) lymphadenopathy can accompany infective processes and should be sought.
citations.source: John Murtagh General Practice, 8th Edition.pdf, p.1809
